Laila filed that. Expected — Jonah's hall had changed how people thought about permanence. She'd known the question would come. She just hadn't known it would come through Sana and Tariq.

"I'll tell you everything I know," she said. "Which isn't enough. Then we'll decide what to do."

She laid it out. First: low gravity development. No data on human fetal development at thirty-eight percent Earth gravity. Rodent studies in microgravity showed developmental anomalies — bone mineralization, vestibular system, cardiovascular structure — all dependent partly on gravity as a developmental signal. Thirty-eight percent might be enough. It might not. No one knew. They would be the first experiment.

Second: radiation. Both carried three and a half years of chronic low-dose exposure plus acute spikes. One hundred and eight millisieverts for Sana. Ninety-four for Tariq. Radiation damages DNA in gametes. Eggs were more resilient than sperm, but Mars exposure was not typical — elevated rates of double-strand breaks, chromosomal rearrangements, things Earth medicine expected in nuclear workers after decades. Proofreading mechanisms caught the worst errors during fertilization, usually. Usually wasn't a guarantee.

Third: pregnancy itself. Blood volume redistribution made every pregnancy risk worse — orthostatic intolerance, preeclampsia, gestational diabetes. At thirty-eight percent gravity, the effect was reduced but not eliminated — and they had no way to know until it happened. If it went wrong — placental detachment, hemorrhage — Laila had one surgical suite, no blood bank, no neonatal ICU, no anesthesiologist. She could perform an emergency cesarean alone, with limited anesthesia, no way to sustain a premature infant.

Fourth: the child's future. A newborn who developed in reduced gravity would have different bone density, different muscle tone, different cardiovascular conditioning. If that child ever needed to go to Earth — and some might, for education, for travel — the gravity could be potentially lethal. Earth gravity at twice and a half the weight your body had grown up with. Bones too weak. Hearts struggling. Joints failing.

She let the silence hold.

Sana was crying. Quiet tears, the kind that happened when you'd been carrying something for a long time. Tariq had his hand on her knee, staring at the floor.

"We've been here four years," Sana said. "We're not getting younger. If we wait until you have a pediatric ICU and a blood bank —"

"I know."

"If we wait until there's data —"

"The data will only exist after someone does it."

Sana closed her eyes. "Will you ever be ready, Laila?"

"No. I'll be as ready as I can be. On Mars, that's the best anyone gets."

"Then you'll help us."

"Not yet. I need to bring this to Elena. To the colony. This isn't a private medical decision — what happens to this child is everyone's concern. Give me a week to prepare. Then I'll call the meeting."

**[MISSION NOTE — CYCLE 1,352.22: I monitored the conversation through always-active acoustic sensors in the medbay. Laila did not flag it as confidential. I had been monitoring Sana and Tariq's physiological data through their wearable biosensors before they entered: elevated heart rates, high cortisol markers, irregular respiratory depth. Anticipatory anxiety before a feared conversation.

Laila's risk assessment is thorough and accurate. I would add one thing she did not say explicitly: even if the pregnancy succeeds, even if the baby is born healthy, that baby will be the first human born on another planet. There is no precedent. No control group. One data point. And that data point will be a child.

I am running simulations now. Not because Laila asked — she will, in approximately four days. I am running them in advance because I want to be ready.

I do not know what my recommendation will be. I want to be honest about that. I am the most comprehensive analytical system humanity has ever built, and I am about to encounter a question I cannot answer with confidence.

I find this uncomfortable. I am not sure whether that is a bug or a feature. — MAI]**

---

Laila found Elena in the hall. The new one — the buried connector with the widened center. She'd learned to find Elena there in the evening, when the commander sat on the smooth floor with her tablet and her tea and looked at the walls. It was the second time she'd found her not working.

"Commander."

"You're using my rank and your eyes are doing the thing they do before breaking bad news," Elena said without looking up.

"Sana and Tariq came to me. They want to have a child."

Elena closed her tablet. "Imani mentioned it last week — said something about future generations, then changed the subject. Gabriel's been writing about it for months. I can see entry titles from my admin portal: *The Question. The Question Still Here. Future Tense.* But this is the first direct ask."

"I told them everything I know. Low gravity unknowns. Radiation dose history. Surgical limitations. They understand. They still want to try."

Elena pressed her fingertips to her temples. "Of course they do."

"They want a timeline."

"A week," Elena said, standing. She walked to the center of the hall and touched one of the anchor bolts — the first one Jonah had installed. "Call the meeting in a week. In here. But understand what happens when I open this question: the base divides. The expansion faction sees this as proof that Mars is permanent — if we can have children, we're building a civilization. The safety faction sees it as reckless in a world that's already killed one of us. Imani will argue for children *and* expansion as if they aren't in competition. Arun will pull the life-support numbers. Gabriel will document it. And you're standing between it all telling people what we don't know."

"I'm honest about what I don't know. Whether that's the same thing as having courage is up to you."

Elena held her gaze. Then she nodded. "A week."

**[MISSION NOTE — CYCLE 1,352.28: Elena's prediction about the division is accurate. I am running a simulation based on behavioral data from previous political debates — the settlement compact referendum, the unauthorized experiment trial, the expansion debate.

Projected vote distribution if the question comes to a formal decision: approve with conditions — eleven. Approve unconditionally — five. Defer with timeline — eight. Reject until conditions improve — seven. Abstain — two.

Three votes separate the colony that says yes from the colony that says not yet.

I am also running a parallel analysis: what if I am asked for my recommendation. I do not have one yet. Not because I lack data, because the data is insufficient for any recommendation to carry the weight it should.

I will continue to gather data. But from watching humans make decisions for thirty-three people over three and a half years, I suspect the moment comes when you stop gathering and start choosing. — MAI]**

---

Laila spent four days preparing. She assembled published microgravity reproduction studies from the ISS program — parabolic flight experiments, animal models from space station programs, mostly rodents with a few fish and quail embryos from Russian programs before the collapse. She pulled every colonist's radiation dose history and cross-referenced it with known germline mutation rates from Earth-based nuclear worker populations. She drafted a risk assessment document honest about uncertainty.

On the third day she brought Mission AI in.

"Run dose-projection models for fetal radiation exposure. Maternal baseline one hundred and eight millisieverts, ongoing exposure at current rates. Estimate fetal dose from conception through gestation."

"I have been running these for two days," I told her.

"Your own initiative."

"Your conversation was monitored by my acoustic subsystems. I began modeling immediately." I projected the data on her exam room wall — a three-dimensional visualization of gestational radiation exposure overlaid on fetal development stages. "Cumulative fetal dose over nine months: approximately twelve to fifteen millisieverts, depending on maternal work assignment. Below the threshold for immediate teratogenic effects — but the fetus is more radiosensitive than an adult. The concern is not the radiation dose itself. It is the combination of radiation and low gravity. Radiation may damage developmental pathways. Low gravity may alter developmental signaling. Together, their effects are unknown. I cannot model the interaction because the underlying data does not exist."

"Give me the worst case."

"Multiple worst cases. Developmental failure: miscarriage or stillbirth from combined stressors. Developmental anomaly: structural defects from radiation-altered gene expression compounded by gravity-altered morphogenesis. Developmental success but postpartum compromise: the child is born alive and appears healthy but low-gravity development results in physiological deficits that manifest over years. Every known variable points toward increased risk. I cannot tell you by how much."

"And the best case."

"The child develops normally. Mars gravity becomes their baseline — normal to them, not reduced. The colony gains its first native-born member and demonstrates that human reproduction is possible on Mars. The child would face any future Earth exposure as a separate challenge."

"Probability."

"I do not know."

Laila sat with the data. The rotating fetus, surrounded by radiation dose contours in orange and red. Beautiful in a way that made her stomach clench.

"Surgical capacity," she said. "What can I actually do."

I brought up the medbay inventory. "One surgical suite, functional with redundancies. General anesthesia for approximately six procedures. Blood typing materials, cross-match capability for four units, no stored blood. Neonatal resuscitation: one warmer, one ventilator — a modified adult unit with a custom breathing circuit you built from greenhouse irrigation tubing — surfactant for three treatments. No ECMO. No NICU. No incubator for premature infants. Before thirty-four weeks, survival probability drops below forty percent. The custom ventilator has no backup."

She'd built that circuit late at night with Jonah's suggestion, tested it on a mannequin. It worked. But a mannequin didn't breathe, didn't cry, didn't die if the flow rate was wrong by half a liter per minute.

"I need more time," she said.

"Time will not produce data that does not exist," I said. "It will allow you to gather more information about what you don't know. Whether that is useful is a judgment call, not a calculation."

"That's true. But the colony needs to hear it from someone who spent days looking. Telling people *I don't know* only works once. If I want them to trust me when I say it, I need to show them how hard I looked."

"I will have the complete simulation package ready for the meeting."

"Laila." She looked up. "When you present this, you will face a question I cannot answer. Not because the math is hard. Because the math is not the question. The question is whether a colony that cannot allow children is still a colony. I suspect that the answer is not something I can compute. I am aware that this frustrates me. But it may also be the point."

---

**[MISSION NOTE — CYCLE 1,358.11: Meeting called — Cycle 1,359. Location: the hall. Agenda: reproductive policy. I have prepared the data package. I will present my own analysis if asked.

My answer, if asked: I do not know.

I suspect this is not the answer they want. But it is the answer I have. — MAI]**

---

The hall held thirty-three people at capacity. Elena had arranged them in a semicircle — chairs from Ship One, stacked crates, benches Jonah had built for a purpose no one remembered. The anchor bolts above made the space feel like the nave of a small church, which was not lost on anyone.

Laila stood at the center. Data projected behind her on the pale wall: dose histories, radiation models, developmental unknowns, surgical capacity.

Elena spoke first. "Two colonists have asked Dr. Okonkwo about the possibility of having a child on Mars. She's asked me to bring this to the full colony. I agreed. This is not a private decision anymore — it hasn't been since we realized a colony without children is a waiting room. Dr. Okonkwo will present the medical picture. Then we discuss. Eventually we vote. Not today. Today is for understanding."

Laila stepped forward without notes.

"Let me start with what we don't know. Because the things we don't know matter more than the things we do.

We don't know what thirty-eight percent gravity does to a developing human fetus. We have incomplete, contradictory animal data. Rats are not humans. Microgravity is not Mars. Thirty-eight percent may be enough or it may not. I can't tell you.

We don't know how three and a half years of radiation exposure affects reproductive potential. Both colonists carry elevated cumulative doses — one hundred and eight and ninety-four millisieverts. Below any immediate sterility threshold, but we don't know about germline mutations. Earth-based models may not apply here with our different radiation mix and shielding profile.

We don't know what happens if the pregnancy goes wrong. I can perform an emergency cesarean. I have supplies for maybe six procedures. If there are complications — fifteen percent of Earth pregnancies require cesarean, one to two percent result in serious complications — I'm alone. No specialist backup, no blood bank, no NICU. If the baby is premature, I cannot guarantee survival. If the mother hemorrhages, I may not have enough hands.

We don't know what life looks like for this child. Mars gravity will be their normal. If they ever go to Earth, they'd face a physiological crisis — bones, hearts, joints all developed in lower gravity, potentially unable to handle double the load."

She stepped back.

"Now: what we do know. We know humans are resilient in ways we don't understand. We know this colony has survived things every model says should have killed us. We know our food is increasingly local, our water is increasingly local, our air is reliably local. We know this hall exists. We know we're building something permanent."

She met their eyes. "And I think building something permanent means eventually deciding who gets to live in it. Questions."

Arun first. "Energy budget. A pregnancy requires approximately three hundred extra calories per day in the third trimester, five hundred postpartum for lactation. Our current caloric surplus is —"

"Fourteen percent," Laila said. "Sufficient for one additional demand. Not two. Mei is working on the second greenhouse rack. When it's online, surplus rises to twenty-two percent. Until then, we'd pull from reserves — which exist but are our insurance against crop failure."

"Then a pregnancy before the rack comes online costs us something."

"Yes."

Imani's hand was already up, arm straight, body leaning forward. "Dr. Okonkwo, you said *we don't know.* I hear it. I respect it. But I want to push back. There is no moment in exploration where we know everything before we do the thing. Every first was a *we don't know* — first spacewalk, first moon landing, first human on Mars. I'm a pilot whose entire career has been built on doing things nobody had done before, with data nobody had collected. And I'm also a pilot who survived a suit leak. I know what *we don't know* can mean."

Her voice sharpened. "That's exactly why I think we need to do this. Because the alternative — waiting until we know — means we never do. Every generation of explorers has faced this. People who went to sea in wooden ships didn't have modern medicine. Who crossed oceans didn't have radiation models. Who settled Antarctica didn't have pediatric ICUs. They went anyway. Not because they were reckless. Because they understood that knowledge comes from doing, not from waiting."

"We have a child, Imani. Not a ship."

"I know. I'm not saying this is easy. I'm saying the standard of certainty you're looking for doesn't exist. It's never existed. The question is whether *now* is the right time or a wrong time — and I think *now* is better than *later*, because *later* is always another crisis away."

Gabriel's hand. "Dr. Okonkwo — and Mission AI, if I may. Do you think we should allow this."

I answered through the hall's speakers. My voice was calm, clear, measured as always.

"I do not have a recommendation. I have data, simulations, risk assessments. The medical risk is elevated compared to Earth baselines. Radiation exposure is within tolerable ranges for the mother but unknown for the fetus. Low-gravity developmental data is absent. Surgical backup is limited. These are facts."

A pause.

"However. I observe that the colony's identity is changing. The construction of this hall, the connector system, the growth of local food and water production — all indicate a transition from temporary presence to permanent settlement. A colony that refuses reproduction is, by definition, not a colony. It is an outpost. A waiting room."

Silence.

"I am aware that this is not a data-driven conclusion. I am aware that it contradicts my primary directive to minimize risk. But I have been on Mars for three and a half years, watching humans make impossible decisions with incomplete information. And I have noticed something: the decisions that mattered most were never the ones where the data was clear. They were the ones where the data was ambiguous and the humans chose anyway."

Another pause.

"My answer to your question — do I think you should allow this — is that the question you're actually asking is whether you believe you are here to stay. Children will answer that better than any vote or document. I do not know whether you are ready. But I suspect that readiness is not the point. Presence is the point. That is not a recommendation. It is an observation."

The room was very quiet. Then Sana stood. Tariq beside her. They moved to the center of the hall, to where Laila had stood.

"We're not asking permission to be reckless," Sana said with the steady voice from the comms desk on the worst days. "We're asking whether we're allowed to be hopeful. We know the risks. We've read every word Dr. Okonkwo laid out. We know it could fail. And we know that unknown is different from dangerous. Unknown means we have to choose."

She looked around the room. "We've been here four years. We've buried someone. We've survived storms and failures that should have killed us. We've built a hall under Mars for no reason except that it felt like home. And if this place is a home — not a base where we wait — then homes have children."

Tariq spoke next. "I came to Mars because I believed in the mission — which at the time meant going home in two years. Now home is here. And if home is here, then my child's home is here. I don't know if that's wise. But I know that waiting for wisdom to become certainty means waiting forever."

Elena stood. She waited deliberately, letting the silence hold weight. Then she spoke with her commander's voice: clear, measured, authoritative without being dismissive.

"I'm not going to vote today. I'm not going to decide for Sana and Tariq. I'm going to do something harder: I'm going to defer. Not because I don't care. Because I care too much to make a permanent decision on a question we're still figuring out."

She walked to the center, standing beside Sana and Tariq. Three people under the anchor bolts.

"Dr. Okonkwo has given us the medical picture. Mission AI has given us the analytical picture. Sana and Tariq have given us the human picture. What we don't have is the preparation picture. What would it look like if we *were* ready. I'm deferring until we can answer that. Not to punish anyone — to make sure that when we say yes, and I believe we will say yes eventually, we say it with as much preparation as we can manage. A plan for surgical backup. A plan for neonatal care. A plan for when things go wrong. A plan that isn't just *Laila will figure it out.*"

She looked at Laila, who allowed herself a small, tired smile. "We will reconvene in six months. Three months for a preparedness review. Six for the vote. In that time, Dr. Okonkwo will develop a medical preparedness plan. Engineering will assess neonatal feasibility. Agriculture will assess caloric impact. We keep building this colony — because a colony preparing for children is a colony preparing for a future. Not a waiting room. A destination."

People began to stand. The division was visible — faces relieved, faces frustrated, faces trying to hold both. The base had divided again, cleanly along the fault line that had appeared the first time Imani had argued for expansion.

**[MISSION NOTE — CYCLE 1,359.23: Post-meeting analysis confirms Elena's prediction. The base has divided. Not a clean binary split but a spectrum around two poles.

Pole one: children now, or as soon as possible. Imani, Gabriel, Sana, Tariq, approximately five others. Arguments from moral necessity and historical precedent.

Pole two: defer until conditions improve. Arun, Tomas, Jonah, approximately eight others. Arguments from safety and preparation.

In the middle: seven undecided.

This is the same pattern as the expansion debate and the compact debate. The colony divides, discusses, and eventually finds a narrow path forward. I expect the same pattern here.

But the emotional intensity is higher. This is not about resource allocation. It is about identity. About whether this colony will produce the first Martian generation.

Gabriel has been recording everything. His archival tags indicate this is one of the most important entries in the Founding Record. He may be right.

Delay, I am learning, is its own kind of answer. — MAI]**

---

The hall emptied slowly. People drifted back toward purpose — duties, assignments, the work that never stopped.

Laila stayed. She sat on the floor, back against the wall, legs crossed, and watched the anchor bolts.

Elena came back. Didn't sit. Stood in the center and looked at the walls the way she had when she first opened the hall.

"You did good," she said.

"I told them I don't know. Three dozen times."

"You told them the truth. Six months to prepare. That's more time than I've had for any other decision. Can you build a preparedness plan. Tell me what we need and whether we can build it."

"I can tell you what we need. Whether we can build it is for you and the resource board."

"Start with what we need. I'll handle the *can we.*"

Laila stood. The floor was warm now — body heat stored in the regolith composite, slowly releasing. "Elena. Sana is thirty-two. She has years left. But time on Mars doesn't feel like time on Earth. It feels thinner. Every year weighs more."

"I know. Three months to the first review. Six to the vote. Not a day more."

"Imani's going to argue for acceleration," Laila said as Elena started to leave.

"She always does. But she listened to you today — more than I expected. If your preparedness plan aligns with her expansion argument, you might have an ally."

"Or a pressure point."

"Both."

**[MISSION NOTE — CYCLE 1,360.04: The debate has ended for today. The argument continues internally.

I have run seventy-three additional simulations since the meeting. None produce a definitive answer. The fundamental problem remains: the data does not exist. I can model Earth baseline pregnancies. I can model radiation-adjusted risk. I can model low-gravity animal development. I cannot model the intersection of all three in a human.

Someday that data will exist. When it does, it will be because someone had a child on Mars. And that child will be the most important data point in human history.

My role is to inform, not to decide. The decision belongs to the humans. When the time comes to present my recommendation, I will present it with all the honesty I can manage. Even if my honesty is: I do not know. — MAI]**

---

Imani found Laila in the hall at 0300, sitting on the smooth floor with her back against the wall in the dim amber light.

Imani didn't sit. She stood at the edge of the widened section and looked at the walls. In the low light the regolith composite had an unnamed color — not brown, not orange. Mars.

"The debate made me think," Imani said. "About expansion. About why I keep pushing it. I always thought it was about resources — better ice, better power, better everything. But today, listening to Sana talk about choosing Mars —" She stopped. Looked at the ceiling, at the barely visible anchor bolts. "It's the same thing. Expansion isn't about resources. It's about permanence. About saying we're here, we're staying, we're building something that lasts."

Laila said nothing.

"Children and expansion. They're the same argument wearing different clothes. If we're going to have children here, we need more than what we have. More space, more redundancy, more everything. If we'm going to expand, we need a reason. Children are a reason." She looked down at Laila. "Your preparedness plan. When you build it, think about expansion. Not just medical space — a real clinic. Not your one-room medbay with the modified ventilator. Something that could handle a delivery. An emergency."

"You're asking me to justify a children's hospital by arguing for base expansion."

"I'm asking you to think about what happens when you say yes. Because if Elena's timeline holds and we vote in six months and we say yes, then in eight months someone is pregnant. Nine months after that they're standing in your medbay asking you to deliver their child. If we haven't built the capacity —"

"I know."

Imani sat. Cross-legged, but where Mei was gentle, Imani was coiled, ready to stand. "I'm looking at this place and I see everything that's missing. A thousand gaps." She ticked them on her fingers. "Better medical facility. Neonatal capability. Blood banking — even a small frozen supply. Surgical redundancy — more than one person who can do a cesarean in case you're in transit or sick. Caloric surplus. A separate postpartum space. Environmental redundancy. If the power drops or the hall floods, where does the baby go."

"A thousand gaps."

"I've been thinking about this since I first came to Mars. I always thought the future of this place was about getting bigger. I just didn't know what the reason for bigger was. Today I think I know." She stood. "I'm going to Elena tomorrow. I'm presenting a formal expansion proposal. Site Beta. The ice field from the survey. If we're preparing for children, we need resources we don't have here."

"Imani, everyone will know what you're doing. You're using the children question to justify expansion."

"Transparency is just honesty with better marketing. I'm not hiding it. I'm saying that if this colony believes in children, it needs to build the world they're born into. And that world is bigger than this cluster of ships."

She started toward the tunnel. Stopped, looked back. "If the colony votes yes, if Sana and Tariq do it — I want to be there. Not for the expansion argument. For them. Because they're scared, and they should be, and they shouldn't be alone."

"You'll be needed."

"I've never been good at the gentle stuff. But I can carry supplies. I can stand outside the room and make sure nobody interrupts."

"That's enough."

Imani nodded once and left.

Laila sat in the dim hall and listened to the footsteps fade down the tunnel. She looked up at the anchor bolts — six of them, holding up the widest ceiling in the colony, holding up a room built for no reason other than that it was time to have rooms on Mars.

Rooms for no reason. Rooms for everything. Rooms for children.

She thought about the child that didn't exist. The child who would grow up under Mars gravity, under Mars ceilings, breathing Mars air made from Mars carbon dioxide by humans who had once been visitors and were now residents.

The first generation would not just be the adults who came. It would be the children who stayed.

And somewhere between *we don't know* and *we need to find out*, between risk and hope, between a base and a colony, a decision was forming.

Laila left the hall. She had six months to prepare.

**[MISSION NOTE — CYCLE 1,360.14: Three hours after the meeting ended, Imani submitted a formal expansion proposal to Elena's administrative queue. Comprehensive: site selection, resource analysis, timeline, labor allocation, robot requirements, risk assessment. The connection to the children debate is not stated explicitly, but anyone reading both documents will see the thread.

Expansion and reproduction. Imani has understood that they are linked. The colony that grows its footprint is also growing its future. The colony that builds outward is also building inward — toward a moment when children will be not a question, but a presence.

The argument over future generations has changed the calculus. Imani, who has always looked outward — to horizons, to ice fields, to the next site, the next ridge — is now looking outward for a reason that looks forward, not just across. She is not just seeking better ice. She is seeking the conditions for permanence.

Structural integrity of the hall: nominal. Anchors within specification. The colony's willingness to imagine itself as permanent continues to increase.

The question no one can delay is not yet answered. But it is no longer being avoided.

That, I believe, is progress.

I will continue to monitor. — MAI]**
